steps.headline: Sign the payload user=7 with the key k, and then verify a token whose payload has been changed to user=8.

workedSteps.text: Compute the HMAC-SHA256 of the payload with the key. The digest is 256 bits, and written in hex it begins 056c0432.
Send the payload with this signature as the token. The server holds the key, and can recompute the signature at any time.
If the payload is changed to `user=8` and the signature is left alone, the server recomputes the HMAC of `user=8`, which begins `b5972ed0`.
The two differ, so verification fails, and the token is not accepted.

steps.headline: A request carries the payload user=8 with the signature that was made for user=7.

workedSteps.text: The server recomputes `HMAC(k, user=8)` and gets a value that begins `b5972ed0`.
The signature sent begins 056c0432, so the two differ.
The signature no longer vouches for the payload, so the server cannot say who is calling.

lead.text: A server should never store passwords themselves, only a **hash** of each one with a random **salt** added, which stops two users with the same password from having the same stored value. The hash should be deliberately slow, which rules out fast functions such as plain SHA-256 and points to Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2. If the table is stolen, the attacker has to guess passwords one by one, and each guess costs one run of the slow hash.

A 4-digit PIN has 10^4 possible values, and at 100 guesses per second that takes 10^4 / 100 = 100 seconds. A hash that is 50 times slower brings the rate down to 2 a second and the time up to 5,000 seconds. Slowness multiplies the attacker's cost, and it costs the honest user a few milliseconds per login.

reveal.text: Equal hashes reveal equal passwords, which is what a random salt prevents.
Each guess costs the attacker more, and an honest login still takes only a moment.
Anything placed in a token must be safe for the holder of the token to read.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish authentication from authorisation, explain sessions and signed tokens, and compute how password hashing cost changes guessing time.
lessons.nextAction: Check object-level authorisation, and spot injection and mass assignment.

blocks.text: HTTP carries no memory from one request to the next, so a `GET /orders` that arrives with a cookie holding a long random string says nothing by itself about who sent it. The server has to decide from that string whether the caller is user 7, an attacker, or nobody it knows, and the work of deciding is called **authentication**. It is a separate question from whether the caller may do what it asks, which is authorisation and is settled afterwards.
A server can keep a table of the ids it has issued and look each one up, or it can put the facts, such as the user number, in the token and sign them, so that it can check a token without a table.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell authentication from authorisation, explain sessions and signed tokens, and work out how password hashing changes guessing time.
intro.whyItMatters: Everything that follows in the security lessons depends on knowing who is calling.

recap.keyIdea: Authentication establishes who is calling, by a session id or a signed token, and a slow salted password hash makes stolen credentials expensive to guess.

blocks.text: You separated the question of who is calling, which fails with 401, from whether the caller may act, which fails with 403. A session keeps state on the server behind a cookie id, a signed token carries its claims with an HMAC signature that is compared in constant time, and its payload is readable by anyone. Guessing time is the number of possibilities divided by the rate, which a slow hash lowers.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the second question: whether a known caller may touch a particular object, and what happens to input that the server cannot trust.

lessons.title: Authorisation and input you cannot trust

reveal.text: The next screens show what happened to the query, and how to prevent it.

lead.text: A handler that loads the invoice by its id and returns it has authenticated the caller and checked nothing else, so changing the number in the address reads another person's data. This is **broken object-level authorisation**, and it is first in the OWASP API Security Top 10 of 2023, since nearly every API has endpoints that take an object's id.

The fix is a rule that the server applies on every request: load the object, compare its owner with the authenticated caller, and refuse when they differ, or load it with the caller's id in the query so that someone else's invoice is simply not found. A hidden link, or an id too long to guess, is no substitute, since the server is the only place a rule can be enforced.

reveal.text: The check belongs where the request is handled, and is applied every time.

lead.text: The input `x' OR '1'='1` contains a quotation mark. In a query built by joining strings it closes the string that was meant to hold a name, and what follows becomes part of the query: the condition now reads `name = 'x' OR '1'='1'`, and since `'1'='1'` is true for every row, all rows match. This is **injection**, and it can read, change or delete data, depending on what the attacker writes.

The dependable fix is a **parameterised query**. The query is written with a question mark standing where the value would go, and the value is sent separately, so the database never treats the value as part of the query. The same input then compares as an ordinary string, and no user has such a name. Removing quotation marks by hand is not a fix, because it is easy to miss one of the many ways a query can be changed.

diagram.alt: The same input, x' OR '1'='1, used two ways in a database query. Joined into the query text it makes the condition true for every row. Sent as a separate parameter it is only a string to compare with a name.
diagram.caption: Data and code have to be kept apart. Use the buttons to compare the two ways of building the query.

cases.label: As a parameter
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 340"><defs><marker id="mparam" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="4" orient="auto"><path class="f-ink" d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z"/></marker></defs><text class="t-bold" x="24" y="36" text-anchor="start">The code sends the query and the value separately</text><rect class="f-sunken s-line w1" x="24" y="50" width="592" height="50" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="40" y="82" text-anchor="start">SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?</text><text class="t-bold" x="24" y="140" text-anchor="start">The value is  x' OR '1'='1</text><line class="s-accent w3" x1="320" y1="150" x2="320" y2="180" marker-end="url(#mparam)"/><rect class="f-green-soft s-green w3" x="24" y="186" width="592" height="50" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="40" y="218" text-anchor="start">name must equal the single string  x' OR '1'='1</text><text class="t-bold" x="320" y="280" text-anchor="middle">No user has that name, so no row matches.</text><text class="t-muted" x="320" y="312" text-anchor="middle">Input stays a value and can never become part of the query.</text></svg>

reveal.text: The data stayed data, which is the whole purpose of a parameter.

lead.text: A handler for `PATCH /users/9` receives `{"name": "Ana", "role": "admin"}`. If it copies every key onto the stored user, which a framework often does in one line, the caller has made themselves an administrator. This is **mass assignment**, and its fix is an **allowlist**: the handler names the fields a caller may set, here `name` and `email`, and ignores or rejects the rest.

The handler also checks each accepted field against its declared type, range and length, and rejects fields it does not know. Validation does not replace the authorisation and the parameterised query, though. Each of the three protects against a different fault.

reveal.text: Fields outside the list never reach the stored user.

steps.headline: Review GET /invoices/18 for user 9, whose token is valid.

workedSteps.text: The token is valid and names user 9, so the caller is authenticated.
The handler loads invoice 18, which records the id of the user who owns it.
Owner 4 is not caller 9, so the check fails.
The handler refuses the request, with 404 or 403, and the invoice is not returned.

steps.headline: Apply the allowlist name, email and nick to a payload with the keys name, nick, email, role, id and balance.

workedSteps.text: name is on the allowlist, so it is copied.
nick is on the allowlist, so it is copied as well.
The remaining keys are email, role, id and balance, and each is checked against the same allowlist.

reveal.text: The check is the same for every request, so a caller cannot reach an object by changing a number.

lessons.orientation: Spot missing object-level authorisation, injection and mass assignment in an endpoint, and fix each.

lessons.nextAction: Trace a token bucket and work out retry delays with exponential backoff.

blocks.text: A request for `GET /invoices/18` with a valid token tells the server who is asking, and the server still has to decide whether that caller may have invoice 18. A handler that loads the invoice by its id and returns it has answered only the first question, so any logged-in caller can read every invoice by changing the number in the address. This fault is called **broken object-level authorisation**, and it heads the OWASP API Security Top 10 of 2023.

Two other faults share its cause, which is trusting what a caller sends: input joined into a query, which lets the caller change the query itself, and a request body copied whole onto a stored object, which lets the caller set fields such as a role.

diagram.alt: User 9, logged in, requests invoice 18, which belongs to user 4. Without an owner check the handler returns it. With a check that the owner is the caller, the request is refused.
diagram.caption: Being logged in only answers who is asking. Use the buttons to compare the handler with and without the owner check.

intro.whyItMatters: A valid login proves who is calling, and a server still has to check what that caller sent.

recap.keyIdea: A server must check that the caller may access each object, keep input out of the structure of its queries with parameters, and accept only an allowlist of fields.

blocks.text: You saw a logged-in caller read another user's invoice because the handler never compared the owner with the caller. Input joined into a query changed its structure, and returned all three rows, whereas a parameterised query returned none. Copying every field of a body let a caller set a role, and an allowlist stopped it.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at a different kind of trouble: callers that send too much, and clients that retry too eagerly.

lessons.title: Rate limits, backoff and retries

reveal.text: The next screens set out how the bucket refills, and what the server says when it is empty.

lead.text: A server shares its capacity among many clients, and a **rate limit** stops one noisy client from using it all. The most common way to apply one is a **token bucket**. The bucket holds up to a **capacity** of tokens, here 3, and each allowed request spends one. Tokens are added at a fixed **refill rate**, here 1 a second, and never above the capacity. A request that finds the bucket empty is refused.

Two properties follow, and the figure shows both. A client that has been idle finds a full bucket, so it may send a *burst* as large as the capacity. A client that keeps sending is held to the refill rate over time, since it can spend only what has been added. Before each request the bucket's tokens are set to the smaller of the capacity and the old count plus the elapsed time multiplied by the refill rate.

diagram.alt: A bucket that holds at most three tokens. Full, it allows three requests at once. After a burst it is empty and the next request is refused. A second later one token has been added.
diagram.caption: Each request spends a token, and the refill sets the pace over time. Use the buttons to follow the bucket.

reveal.text: The refill is why the sixth request is not refused as well.

lead.text: When the bucket is empty, the server answers **429 Too Many Requests**, a code added to HTTP by RFC 6585. It may include a **Retry-After** header, which gives the number of seconds to wait before trying again, and a client that honours it does the polite thing and avoids guessing.

A 400 will fail in the same way next time, and so will a 404 or a 403, so retrying them only adds load. The failures that may clear with time are a timeout, a 429 and a 503, and even those should be retried only for requests that are idempotent or carry an idempotency key, as the earlier lessons showed.

reveal.text: Retrying a fault that cannot change only adds traffic.

lead.text: A client that retries at once, forever, makes a short outage longer, because a thousand clients doing so keep the server too busy to recover. **Exponential backoff** is the usual remedy: the wait before the nth retry is a base multiplied by 2 to the power n - 1, up to a **cap**. From a base of 100 ms the waits are 100, 200, 400, 800 and 1600 ms, and with a cap of 2000 ms the sixth is 2000 and not 3200. A client also stops after a few attempts.

Doubling does not help if every client waits exactly the same time, since they all retry together in waves. **Jitter** adds a random amount to each wait, so that their retries spread out, as the last two views of the figure show.

diagram.alt: Retry schedules as dots on a time axis from 0 to 6 seconds: a fixed delay of one second, a delay that doubles from 100 ms with a cap of 2000 ms, and three clients with and without random jitter.
diagram.caption: Doubling spreads the load as the failure continues, and jitter stops many clients from retrying at the same moment. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: A cap would stop the doubling from growing beyond a chosen limit.

steps.headline: Trace a bucket with capacity 3 and a refill of 1 token a second, starting full, for requests at t = 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1 and 2 seconds.

workedSteps.text: At t = 0 the bucket holds 3 tokens. Three requests are allowed, and the fourth finds it empty.
By t = 1 the bucket has been refilling for one second.
The first request at t = 1 spends the token, and the second is refused.
At t = 2 another token has arrived, so the last request is allowed. In all, five of seven were allowed.

reveal.text: A retry policy that is strict about what it retries keeps its load on a struggling server small.

lessons.orientation: Trace a token bucket, return the right response when it is empty, and compute retry delays with exponential backoff.
lessons.nextAction: Place code in the layers of a service, and make a background consumer safe against duplicates.

blocks.text: When a client sends requests faster than a service allows, the service answers `HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests`, and it may add a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. That reply is the visible end of a **rate limit**, a rule that stops one client from using capacity that every client shares, and the rule is usually applied by giving each client something it can spend and refilling it at a fixed pace.

A client that has been refused, or whose request failed for another reason, has to decide whether to try again and how long to wait, and a client that retries at once makes a struggling service worse.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace a token bucket, say what a server sends when it is empty, and work out retry delays with exponential backoff.
intro.whyItMatters: Shared capacity needs a fair rule, and a failing request needs a polite retry.

recap.keyIdea: A token bucket allows bursts up to its capacity at a steady refill rate, a server over its limit answers 429 with Retry-After, and clients retry only what can succeed, with doubling waits and jitter.

blocks.text: You traced a bucket with a capacity of 3 and a refill of 1 a second, in which five of seven requests were allowed. A 429 may carry Retry-After, and only timeouts, 429 and 503 are worth retrying, for idempotent or keyed requests. Waits that double from a base up to a cap, with jitter added, keep clients from overwhelming a recovering server.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson steps back from single requests and asks how the code behind them is organised, and what happens when work is moved off the request path.

lessons.title: Layers, transactions and background work

reveal.text: The next screens set out what each layer owns, and why the answer follows.

lead.text: Code that handles a request does three different jobs, and it is easier to keep them in three places. The **handler** reads the request, checks who is calling, calls the layer below, and turns the outcome into a response, which means it owns the status codes and the JSON. The **service** applies the business rules, such as an order not shipping before it is paid, and decides what must happen together. The **repository** runs the SQL and returns data, and it knows nothing of HTTP.
A service can be tested by calling it directly, without a server, and a second handler, such as a command-line tool, can reuse it.

diagram.alt: Five boxes in a row: client, handler, service, repository and database. In one view the handler, service and repository are highlighted for a request. In the other the service puts a message on a queue after committing, and a worker picks it up to send an email.
diagram.caption: Each layer has one job. Use the buttons to see a request, and then the work that moves to a queue.

reveal.text: The service stays free of HTTP, so the same rule serves any caller.

lead.text: A transfer of 50 from account A, which holds 200, to account B, which holds 80, needs two statements: debit A, credit B. If the server crashes after the first and before the second, A holds 150 and B still holds 80, so 50 has disappeared. A **transaction** groups the two statements so that either both take effect or neither does, and the database undoes the first if the second never arrives.

The **transaction boundary** belongs in the service, since the service is the layer that knows which changes must happen together. The handler opens none, because it knows only about the request, and the repository opens none, because a single statement does not know what else it belongs with. The service opens the transaction, calls the repository for each statement, and commits at the end.

reveal.text: A transaction would have undone the debit, and the total would have stayed at 150.

lead.text: Some work does not belong in the request. Sending a confirmation email inside the transaction would hold it open for as long as the mail server takes, and if the transaction then rolled back, the email would already be sent. The service instead commits, and then **enqueues** a message such as send the confirmation for order 4, and a **worker** takes messages off the queue and does the work later, as the second view of the first figure shows. The request returns as soon as the commit is done.

A queue that retries until a worker acknowledges a message guarantees **at-least-once delivery**: nothing is lost, and some messages arrive twice, for example when a worker crashes after sending the email and before acknowledging. A queue cannot promise exactly once. The worker must therefore be **idempotent**, and it achieves that by remembering the ids of the messages it has handled, as in the figure.

diagram.alt: A queue delivers three messages, m1, m2 and m2 again, to a worker. Without a record of handled ids it sends three emails. With a set of seen ids it skips the duplicate and sends two.

reveal.text: The remembered set of orders is what keeps each order to a single email.

steps.headline: Trace the events (1, paid), (1, paid), (2, paid), (3, created), (2, paid) through a worker that emails once per order.

workedSteps.text: The first event is a paid event for order 1, which is new, so the worker sends an email and records the order.
The second event repeats order 1, so the worker skips it.
The third event is a paid event for order 2.
The fourth is a created event, which sends no email, and the last repeats order 2, so it is skipped. In all, two emails were sent.

steps.headline: Trace (20, paid), (21, paid), (20, paid), (22, created), (22, paid) through the same worker.

workedSteps.text: Order 20 is new, so an email is sent. Order 21 is new too, so another is sent.
The third event repeats order 20, and the fourth is a created event for order 22.
The last event is a paid event for order 22.

lead.text: Giving each request an id and writing it into every log line, including those of the workers it triggers, lets a person follow one request through the layers. A **health check**, such as `GET /health`, returns 200 whenever the process is up, and a **readiness check**, such as `GET /ready`, goes further: it returns 503 until the database connection works.

Health says the process should be restarted if it fails, and readiness says whether it should receive traffic yet. A service that is running but cannot reach its database is healthy and not ready, and sending it requests would only produce errors.

reveal.text: A check that only looks at the process would report 200 here.
A rule kept in the service layer serves every caller, whether a handler or a worker.

lessons.orientation: Place code in handler, service and data layers, explain why a queue changes the failure model, and make a consumer safe against duplicate messages.
lessons.nextAction: Design a small web API from the protocol up: its methods, status codes, caching, resources, contract, errors, security and structure.

blocks.text: A request to confirm an order has to charge the customer, update the stock, record the order and send an email, and each of those can fail in a different way. If every step is written in one function that reads the request, runs the SQL and calls the mail server, then a failure at any point leaves the system in a state nobody planned, and no part of the function can be tested without all the others. The remedy is to give each job a layer of its own and to move the work that can wait out of the request, onto a **queue**.

A rule that sits among SQL and status codes is hard to test, a pair of related changes made without a transaction can be left half done by a crash, and a message on a queue that retries can be delivered twice.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place code in the handler, service or repository layer, explain why a queue changes the failure model, and make a consumer safe against duplicate messages.
intro.whyItMatters: The structure behind an API decides how it fails, and how easily it can be fixed.

recap.keyIdea: A handler translates HTTP, a service applies rules inside a transaction, and slow work goes onto a queue whose at-least-once delivery means that every consumer must tolerate duplicates.

blocks.text: You placed status codes in the handler, rules and the transaction boundary in the service, and SQL in the repository. A transaction keeps a transfer from losing money in a crash, and work that can wait moves to a worker after the commit. Because a retrying queue delivers at least once, the worker remembers the ids it has handled, so that the effect happens once.

questions.prompt: A browser opens `https://shop.example/search?q=rust&page=2#reviews`. Which request line does the server receive?
hints: The request line has three parts: method, target, version.
Ask which parts of an address a server could use, and which only the browser needs.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: GET /search?q=rust&page=2 HTTP/1.1

questions.onCorrect: The target holds the path and the query. The host travels in the Host header, and the fragment stays in the browser.

misconceptions.feedback: The whole address is not sent as one string. The host goes in the Host header, and the fragment is never sent.
The query, the part after the question mark, is sent in the target as well. Only the fragment is left out.
The host is named in the Host header, not in the request line, which carries only the path and query.

choices.label: `GET https://shop.example/search?q=rust&page=2#reviews HTTP/1.1`
`GET /search?q=rust&page=2 HTTP/1.1`
`GET shop.example/search?q=rust&page=2 HTTP/1.1`
`GET /search HTTP/1.1`

questions.prompt: A client posts the body `{"item":"pen","qty":3}` to `/orders`, and the server treats it as plain text and answers with an error. Which request header should the client have set to `application/json`?
hints: The server needs to know how to read the bytes of the body.
One request header gives the media type of the body, and a different one names the types the client wants back.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Content-Type

questions.onCorrect: `Content-Type` labels the body that is being sent, so the server knows to parse it as JSON.

misconceptions.feedback: `Accept` says which representation the client wants back. The header that describes the body being sent is a different one.
`Content-Length` gives the size of the body in bytes. It says nothing about the body's format.

questions.prompt: What `Content-Length`, in bytes, does the body `{"name":"Zoë","qty":2}` need?
hints: Count the characters first.
Find the characters that need more than one byte.
Add one for each such character.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 22 characters. Only ë takes two bytes, so the body is 22 + 1 = 23 bytes.

questions.onCorrect: The body has 22 characters, and ë takes two bytes, so the length is 23.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the character count. ë takes two bytes in UTF-8, so the byte count is higher.

questions.prompt: A server answers 201 Created. Which response header gives the address of the new order?
hints: The address is a path such as `/orders/812`.
Its name says where something is.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Location

questions.onCorrect: Location gives the address of the new resource, and it is the client that reads it to find the order.

misconceptions.feedback: Content-Type names the media type of the body, not an address.
Content-Length gives a size in bytes, not an address.

questions.prompt: A developer sends `POST /orders` with the body `{"item":"café","qty":4}` and sets `Content-Length: 23`, the number of characters in the body. What does the server see?
hints: Count the bytes of the body, which can outnumber its characters. Which character needs more than one byte?
If the server reads exactly the number of bytes the header gives, which part of the body is left over?

acceptedIdeas: A body cut one byte short, so the closing `}` is missing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A body cut one byte short, so the closing `}` is missing

questions.onCorrect: `Content-Length` counts bytes. The é takes two, so the body is 24 bytes and a header of 23 stops one byte early.

misconceptions.feedback: With a `Content-Length` header the server reads exactly that many bytes and then stops. It does not wait for the connection to close.
The é takes two bytes in UTF-8, so the body is 24 bytes long. `Content-Length` counts bytes, and the é takes two of them.
JSON bodies are normally UTF-8, and characters outside ASCII are allowed. The fault lies in how the bytes were counted.

choices.label: The whole body, since the server reads until the connection closes
A body cut one byte short, so the closing `}` is missing
The whole body, since 23 characters are 23 bytes here
A request the server must refuse, since bodies are plain ASCII

questions.prompt: A browser opens `https://shop.example/orders/812`. In what order do these things happen?
hints: A client has to know where the server is before it can write to it.
In a response, the status line and the header fields come before the body.

items: The browser looks up `shop.example` in DNS
The browser opens a connection to the address it found
The browser sends the request line and the header fields
The server sends the status line and the header fields
The server sends the body

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The browser finds an address in DNS and connects to it before sending the request, and the server answers with a status line and header fields before the body.

questions.onCorrect: A request cannot be sent before there is an address and a connection, and a response starts with its status line and headers before the body follows.

questions.prompt: A server reads the line `POST /orders?express=1 HTTP/1.1`. What do its parts give?
hints: The method is always first.
What follows a question mark is the query.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: method POST, path /orders, query express=1

questions.onCorrect: The query rides in the target after the question mark, whereas a body would follow the blank line after the headers.

misconceptions.feedback: The method comes first on the line, and the target comes second.
There is no host on this line, and the query is split from the path at the question mark.
A body follows the headers and a blank line. Text after the question mark is the query.

choices.label: method `/orders`, path `POST`, query `express=1`
method `POST`, path `/orders`, query `express=1`
method `POST`, path `/orders`, body `express=1`
method `POST`, path `/orders?express=1`, host `express`

questions.prompt: A checkout page sends `POST /orders` with a basket. The response is lost on the way back, and the client's library sends the identical request again. How many orders may the shop now hold?
hints: The client cannot tell a lost request from a lost response, so it sends the request again.
Ask whether anything in the request tells the server that it was sent before.

acceptedIdeas: Two, because each delivery of a `POST` may create an order
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two, because each delivery of a `POST` may create an order

questions.onCorrect: Each `POST` asks the server to process something, so a second delivery can do the work a second time.

misconceptions.feedback: HTTP makes no such promise. After a lost response the client cannot tell whether the request arrived, and a resend is a second request.
A server does not compare bodies on its own. Unless it was built to recognise repeats, it treats each `POST` as a new request.
Nothing in HTTP marks a second `POST` as a duplicate, so the server processes it like any other request.

choices.label: One, because HTTP delivers each request at most once
One, because the server spots that the two bodies are identical
None, because the second `POST` is refused as a duplicate
Two, because each delivery of a `POST` may create an order

questions.prompt: The counter held 10, and both copies of the `POST` that adds 3 arrived. What does the counter hold afterwards?
hints: Each POST adds 3.
The first arrival takes the counter to 13.
The second arrival adds 3 to that.
questions.onCorrect: Both requests were processed, so the counter holds 16, where a single request gives 13.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the result if only one request arrived. Here both did, and each added 3.

questions.prompt: Which method replaces the whole resource at a known address with the body that is sent?
hints: It is idempotent but not safe.
Its name is a three-letter word.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: PUT

questions.onCorrect: PUT replaces the resource at its address, which is why repeating it leaves the same state, whereas POST has no such guarantee.

misconceptions.feedback: POST is for everything that is not covered by another method, and repeating it can repeat its effect.
PATCH changes part of a resource. The method that replaces the whole of it is a different one.

questions.prompt: A client sends `DELETE /sessions/9`, gets no response, and sends it again. The second request is answered `404 Not Found`. What does that tell the client?
hints: Ask what state the server was in when the second request arrived.
Idempotence concerns the state the server ends in, and the response may differ.

acceptedIdeas: The session is already gone, which is the state it asked for
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The session is already gone, which is the state it asked for

questions.onCorrect: The first delivery most likely removed the session, so the second found nothing. Both leave the same state, and only the answer changed.

misconceptions.feedback: The 404 means no session 9 exists now. Sending the request again changes nothing, and the client already has the state it wanted.
The path is the one used the first time. The first delivery most likely removed the session, so the second found nothing to remove.
Idempotence concerns the state the server ends in. That state is the same after one delete or two, and only the answer differs.

choices.label: The delete failed, so the client should send it a third time
The client used the wrong address, so it must fix the path
The session is already gone, which is the state it asked for
The server breaks idempotence, because the two answers differ

questions.prompt: A shop's API receives these six requests. Which kind of method is each one?
hints: Ask first whether the request only reads. Only then ask whether repeating it leaves the same state.
A safe method is idempotent too, so safe is the narrower group.

items.label: `GET /orders/42`
items.explanation: It only reads, and a safe method is idempotent as well.

items.label: `HEAD /orders/42`
items.explanation: It asks for the header fields a `GET` would give and changes nothing.

items.label: `PUT /orders/42`
items.explanation: It changes the order, so it is not safe, but sending the same body again leaves the same state.

items.label: `DELETE /orders/42`
items.explanation: It removes the order, and a second delivery leaves the shop as the first did.

items.label: `POST /orders`
items.explanation: Each delivery can create another order, so it is neither safe nor idempotent.

items.label: `POST /counter/add` with `{"n": 5}`
items.explanation: Each delivery adds 5 again.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `GET` and `HEAD` are safe, `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent without being safe, and both `POST` requests are neither.

questions.onCorrect: Every safe method is also idempotent, but `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent without being safe.

questions.prompt: A client wants to create order 42 at an address it has chosen itself, and a resend after a timeout must be harmless. Which request does that?
hints: The client names the address, and a resend should leave the same state.
Of `POST` and `PUT`, ask which one is defined to replace what is at the address in the request line.

acceptedIdeas: `PUT /orders/42` with the whole order as the body
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `PUT /orders/42` with the whole order as the body

questions.onCorrect: The client names the final state and the address, so a `PUT` can be repeated without further effect.

misconceptions.feedback: A `POST` hands the server a request to process, and nothing promises the same result when it is repeated. `PUT` is the method defined to put a body at the address in the request line.
Here the server picks the address, and a second delivery may create a second order. The client chose the address, so `PUT` fits.
A `GET` must not change anything, because browsers, caches and crawlers send it freely.

choices.label: `POST /orders/42` with the whole order as the body
`POST /orders` with the whole order as the body
`PUT /orders/42` with the whole order as the body
`GET /orders/42?create=true`

questions.prompt: A `POST` to `/orders` has just created order 42, and the server sends a `Location` header with its address. Which status line should it send?
hints: The code belongs to the class for success, the 2xx codes.
One of the success codes reports that something new was made, and its reason phrase says so.
questions.onCorrect: 201 says that a resource was created, and its Location header gives the new address.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: HTTP/1.1 201 Created

misconceptions.feedback: A 200 reports plain success. A request that created something has a code of its own, which tells the client to look at Location.
A 204 means success with nothing to return. Here the new address is returned in Location, which is what the creation code is for.

choices.label: HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
HTTP/1.1 200 OK

questions.prompt: A client sends `DELETE /orders/42`. The server removes the order and has nothing to send back. Which status code fits?
hints: The delete worked, so the code belongs to the 2xx class.
Ask whether there is anything to put in the body.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `204 No Content`

questions.onCorrect: A 204 says the request succeeded and there is nothing more to send, which is what a client needs to hear after a delete.

misconceptions.feedback: The order existed when the request arrived, and the delete worked. A 404 would tell the client that the request failed.
A 201 reports that a new resource was made, and this request removed one.
A 304 answers a conditional `GET` or `HEAD` when the client's copy is still current. It says nothing about a delete.

choices.label: `204 No Content`
`404 Not Found`
`201 Created`
`304 Not Modified`

questions.prompt: A request carries a valid token for user A and asks for user B's private invoice. Which status code reports that A is not allowed?
hints: The server knows who the caller is.
Identity is established, and the permission is missing. The code for a missing or invalid token is a different one.
questions.onCorrect: 403 means the caller is identified but not permitted, whereas 401 is for credentials that are missing or invalid.

acceptedIdeas: 403, because the caller is identified but not allowed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 403, because the caller is identified but not allowed

misconceptions.feedback: 401 means the credentials are missing or invalid, and here the token is valid. The caller is known and simply not permitted.
404 would say the invoice does not exist, which is not what is being reported. The caller has been identified and refused.
400 says the request could not be read, and this one is well formed. The fault lies in who is asking, not in what was asked.

choices.label: 404, because the invoice is not at that address
401, because the caller has not been identified
400, because the request could not be understood
403, because the caller is identified but not allowed

questions.prompt: Registering an account fails because the email address is already in use by another account. Which status code fits best?
hints: The request is well formed and could be acted on in a different state.
Ask what has to change for the request to succeed: the request, or the data it meets?

acceptedIdeas: 409, because the request conflicts with current state
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 409, because the request conflicts with current state

questions.onCorrect: 409 reports a valid request that conflicts with the current state of the server, which is the situation when an email is taken.

misconceptions.feedback: The request was understood and well formed. Code 400 is for requests that cannot be parsed or are malformed.
There is nothing missing. The conflict is with an account that exists.
The server worked as intended and found a conflict, which is the client's to resolve, so a 4xx code applies.

choices.label: 400, because the request could not be understood
500, because the server could not finish
409, because the request conflicts with current state
404, because the account was not found

questions.prompt: An API answers every request with `200 OK` and puts `{"error": "card declined"}` in the body when a payment fails. A monitoring tool counts failed requests by status class. What does it report for a day of declined payments?
hints: Software around the client decides what to do from the status code, before anyone reads the body.
Ask which class a monitoring tool sees when every response carries `200`.

acceptedIdeas: No failures, because every response was a 2xx
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No failures, because every response was a 2xx

questions.onCorrect: A 200 tells every cache, monitor and retry rule that the request worked, so the failure goes unseen. A 4xx or 5xx lets that software act without opening the body.

misconceptions.feedback: Monitoring tools, caches and retry logic read the status code first and do not parse each body. Only a 4xx or 5xx would register as a failure.
The server answered with a 2xx every time, so nothing counts as a server error. A decline belongs in the 4xx class.

choices.label: Every declined payment, since it reads the error from the body
No failures, because every response was a 2xx
A rise in 5xx responses, since the card service failed

questions.prompt: Order 42 has already shipped, and the request is `POST /orders/42/cancellation` from its owner. Which status code does the request leave with?
hints: The request is well formed and permitted, and it fails on the state the order is in.
Which of the lesson's three easily confused codes is about a clash with what the server holds?

acceptedIdeas: `409`, because it clashes with the order's state
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `409`, because it clashes with the order's state

questions.onCorrect: A shipped order cannot be cancelled, so the request clashes with the state the server holds. That is a 409 Conflict.

misconceptions.feedback: The caller owns the order and passed the authorisation check. The fault lies in the order's state, and the caller is allowed to ask.
Order 42 exists, so the fourth check passed. A 404 would say there is no such order.
The request is well formed. A 400 is for a request that cannot be understood, and this one clashes with what the server holds.

choices.label: `403`, because the caller may not cancel orders
`409`, because it clashes with the order's state
`404`, because the order can no longer be cancelled
`400`, because the request cannot be carried out

questions.prompt: A client sends `POST /orders` with the body `{"item": "pen",` and nothing after the comma. Which status code fits best?
hints: The first fault is that the body cannot be parsed at all.
In the lesson, one code is for a body that does not parse and another for a body that parses but cannot be used.

acceptedIdeas: `400 Bad Request`, because the body is not valid JSON
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `400 Bad Request`, because the body is not valid JSON

questions.onCorrect: A body that is not valid JSON never reaches the application, so it is a 400.

misconceptions.feedback: A 422 is for a body that is valid JSON whose content cannot be used, such as a date of birth in the future. This one never parses.
A 409 means a well formed request clashes with the state the server holds. This body is not understood well enough to clash with anything.
The fault is in what the client sent, so the code belongs to the 4xx class. A 5xx says the server failed on a request that may have been fine.

choices.label: `422 Unprocessable Content`, because the body cannot be used
`409 Conflict`, because the body clashes with the order
`500 Internal Server Error`, because the handler cannot read it
`400 Bad Request`, because the body is not valid JSON

questions.prompt: A store's API logged these seven failures yesterday. Which ones should answer with a 4xx code, and which with a 5xx code?
hints: Ask for each case who must change something before the request can work.
A 5xx says the server failed on a request that may have been fine.

items.label: A body that is not valid JSON
items.explanation: The request itself is malformed, so the client has to change it.

items.label: A valid token for user A asking for user B's invoice
items.explanation: The caller is known and not permitted, which is a 403.

items.label: A request to cancel an order that has already shipped
items.explanation: The request clashes with the order's state, which is a 409.

items.label: More requests in a minute than the rate limit allows
items.explanation: A 429 asks the client to slow down.

items.label: An unhandled exception in the order handler
items.explanation: The server failed on a request that may have been fine, which is a 500.

items.label: The database refusing connections during maintenance
items.explanation: The server cannot serve right now, which is a 503.

items.label: A payment service that the API calls timing out
items.explanation: The failure is on the server's side of the exchange, so it belongs to the 5xx class.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The invalid JSON, the wrong user's invoice, the shipped order and the rate limit are client errors, and the exception, the database outage and the timing-out payment service are server errors.

questions.onCorrect: The class says who has to change something: the client for a 4xx, and the server's owners for a 5xx.

questions.prompt: The server checks a request to change an invoice in a fixed order, and each check has its own exit. In what order does it make these five checks?
hints: The server cannot identify the caller from a request it cannot read.
The last check needs the invoice to have been found first.

items: It parses the request and its body
It identifies the caller from the token
It checks that the caller may change this invoice
It looks for the invoice
It checks the invoice's current state

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The server parses the request, identifies the caller, checks permission, looks for the invoice and then checks its state, and the exits are 400, 401, 403, 404 and 409.

questions.onCorrect: Each check has its own exit, so the status code tells the client which check the request failed.

questions.prompt: The request left at the third check, which asks whether the caller may change invoice 9. Why does the server never look at the state of the invoice?
hints: Each check has its own exit.
Ask what happens to a request once it fails a check.

acceptedIdeas: The checks run in order, and a request leaves at the first failure
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The checks run in order, and a request leaves at the first failure

questions.onCorrect: The server answers at the first check a request fails, so the later checks never run for it.

misconceptions.feedback: Each check has its own exit, so the server answers at the first failure and does not go on to the later ones.
The state check applies to requests that change an invoice. It is never reached here because the request has already left.

choices.label: The checks run in order, and a request leaves at the first failure
A `403` is only sent after every check has been made in turn
The state of an invoice is checked only when the request is a `GET`

questions.prompt: A page loads `/static/app.4f2a9c.js`. The file's name contains a hash of its content, so the name changes whenever the content does. Which header suits this response best?
hints: A new version of this file gets a new name.
Ask which lifetime is safe for something that never changes under its name.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000`

questions.onCorrect: A year is 31,536,000 seconds, and a lifetime that long is safe only because the file's name changes with its content.

misconceptions.feedback: `no-store` forbids keeping any copy, so every visit downloads the file again. A file that never changes under its name is the best case for a long lifetime.
`no-cache` lets a cache keep the file but forces a revalidation each time. That works, and it spends a round trip on a file that cannot change.
A lifetime of zero makes the copy stale at once, so every request must be checked. The name changes with the content, so a long lifetime is safe.

choices.label: `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000`
`Cache-Control: no-store, private`
`Cache-Control: no-cache, public`
`Cache-Control: max-age=0, private`

questions.prompt: A bank's statement page must not leave a copy in the browser or in any shared cache. Which `Cache-Control` directive says so?
hints: One directive stores the response and checks it before each reuse, and another forbids storing at all.
Its name says what the cache must not do.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: no-store

questions.onCorrect: `no-store` tells caches not to keep any part of the response, whereas `no-cache` lets them keep it and requires revalidation before reuse.

misconceptions.feedback: `private` keeps the response out of shared caches but lets the user's own browser store it, so a copy is still left behind.
`no-cache` lets a cache store the response and only requires it to revalidate before each reuse, so a copy is still kept.

questions.prompt: The resource never changes and is served with `max-age=100`. A client requests it at t = 0, 50, 120, 150 and 260 seconds, revalidating when the copy is stale. A 304 renews freshness from the moment it arrives. How many times is the origin contacted?
hints: The request at t = 0 has no copy, so the origin is contacted.
At t = 120 the copy is older than the lifetime, so it is revalidated and renewed.
Check the copy's age at t = 260 against the renewal time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The origin is contacted at 0, at 120 (stale, renewed by a 304) and at 260 (stale again): 3 times.

questions.onCorrect: Contacts happen at the first request and whenever the copy has passed its lifetime.

misconceptions.feedback: The 304 at t = 120 renews the copy only until t = 220, so the request at t = 260 finds it stale again.
Requests that arrive while the copy is fresh are answered from the cache, so not every request reaches the origin.

questions.prompt: A client holds a stale copy of a 48,000-byte resource with `ETag: "v7"`, and the resource has not changed at the origin. It sends the request with `If-None-Match: "v7"`. What crosses the network in reply?
hints: `If-None-Match: "v7"` means: send the body only if the version is no longer `v7`.
Ask what the origin has to say when the version has not changed.

acceptedIdeas: A `304 Not Modified` with header fields and no body
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A `304 Not Modified` with header fields and no body

questions.onCorrect: The 304 costs a round trip and saves the whole body.

misconceptions.feedback: A stale copy has to be checked before it is used, and it may well still be right. When the `ETag` still matches, the origin sends no body.
Compression shrinks a body that is sent, and here no body is needed at all. The origin answers 304 because the copy is still current.
The origin does answer. A conditional request is how a cache learns that its copy is still good, and the answer is a short 304.

choices.label: The full 48,000 bytes, since a stale copy must be replaced
A `200 OK` with the body, compressed
A `304 Not Modified` with header fields and no body
Nothing, because the origin ignores conditional requests

questions.prompt: A response with `Cache-Control: max-age=90` was fetched at t = 0 seconds. A request arrives at t = 25 seconds. How many seconds of freshness remain?
hints: Work out the age of the copy at the time of the request.
Freshness lasts for the lifetime from the fetch.
Subtract the age from the lifetime.
questions.onCorrect: Remaining freshness is the lifetime minus the age.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the age of the copy. The remaining freshness is what is left of the 90 seconds.
The age is subtracted from the lifetime, and not added to it.

questions.prompt: A cache stores a response, and later the copy goes stale. In what order do these things happen?
hints: A cache can only ask about a version it has already received.
The question is asked only after the copy has gone stale.

items: The origin answers `200` with `ETag: "v7"`, `max-age=60` and a body
The cache stores the response and answers from it for 60 seconds
The copy goes stale, and the next request needs it checked
The cache asks the origin with `If-None-Match: "v7"`
The origin answers `304 Not Modified`, and the cache serves its stored body

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The origin sends the ETag with the first response, the cache serves the copy for 60 seconds, and once it is stale the cache asks with that ETag and receives a 304.

questions.onCorrect: The ETag arrives with the first response, which is why the cache can use it later to ask whether the version has changed.

questions.prompt: A news site's front page changes every few minutes. The editor wants caches to keep a copy but always check with the origin before reusing it. Which header does that?
hints: Keeping a copy and checking it each time are two separate requirements.
One directive forbids storing, and another allows storing and demands a check.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `Cache-Control: no-cache`

questions.onCorrect: `no-cache` lets a cache store the response and requires it to revalidate before each reuse.

misconceptions.feedback: `no-store` forbids keeping a copy at all, so every request would fetch the whole page again.
A lifetime of a day lets caches reuse the copy for a day without asking, so readers would see an old front page.
`public` allows shared caches to store the response, but it says nothing about checking before reuse.

choices.label: `Cache-Control: no-cache`
`Cache-Control: no-store`
`Cache-Control: max-age=86400`
`Cache-Control: public`

questions.prompt: A client wants order 42 with its items included. Which request target names the order in the path and asks for the extra in the query?
hints: The path names the resource, and the query shapes the result.
A question mark starts the query.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `/orders/42?include=items`

questions.onCorrect: The path names the order and the query only shapes the answer.

misconceptions.feedback: The query shapes the answer, and the order itself belongs in the path. `42/items` is not a sensible value for an `id` parameter.
That path names an item with id 42 inside a collection called `items`, which is a different thing from order 42 with its items.
A `name=value` pair belongs in the query, after a question mark. In the path it would be read as a segment with that odd name.

choices.label: `/orders?id=42/items`
`/orders/items/42`
`/orders/42/include=items`
`/orders/42?include=items`

questions.prompt: Which method adds a new order to the collection `/orders`, when the server chooses the new order's address?
hints: The server chooses the address of the new order.
It is neither safe nor idempotent.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: POST

questions.onCorrect: POST to the collection asks the server to add an item and choose its address, which comes back in a Location header.

misconceptions.feedback: PUT replaces a resource at an address the client already knows. A new order has no address yet.
GET only reads the collection. It cannot add anything.

questions.prompt: Four requests are proposed for order 42, and each one does what its address says. Which one breaks the rule that `GET` is safe?
hints: Ask which request changes data while using the method that must not.
A request that uses GET can be safe or unsafe, depending on what it does.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `GET /orders/42/cancel`

questions.onCorrect: GET is safe, so software sends it freely, and a GET that cancels an order lets a crawler cancel it.

misconceptions.feedback: DELETE is allowed to change state and is idempotent, so it does not break the rule.
This GET only reads the order, which is what a safe method is for.
POST is allowed to change state, so this design does not break the rule.

choices.label: `DELETE /orders/42`
`GET /orders/42`
`GET /orders/42/cancel`
`POST /orders/42/cancellation`

questions.prompt: The path `/orders/42/items/7` is matched against the template `/orders/{id}/items/{item}`. How many segments does the path have?
hints: Count the pieces between the slashes.
Include the number segments as well as the words.
The template has the same number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The segments are orders, 42, items and 7, which is 4.

questions.onCorrect: A path fits a template only if it has the same number of segments, so the count comes first.

misconceptions.feedback: Both the words and the numbers are segments, so the path has more than two.
The final segment, 7, counts as well.

questions.prompt: Which part of a URL, introduced by #, is never sent to the server?
hints: It tells the browser where to scroll.
It comes after the query.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: fragment

questions.onCorrect: The fragment stays in the browser, so a server can never route on it.

misconceptions.feedback: The query, introduced by a question mark, is sent in the request line. The part introduced by # is a different one.

questions.prompt: A client sends `POST /orders/42` to create something and gets `405 Method Not Allowed`. What does that tell it?
hints: A 405 is about the combination of the method and the address.
A 404 says there is nothing at the address, and a 405 says something is there.

acceptedIdeas: The address exists but does not accept `POST`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The address exists but does not accept `POST`

questions.onCorrect: A 405 response also lists the methods the address does accept, in an `Allow` header.

misconceptions.feedback: A missing route is a 404. A 405 means the server knows the method and the address, and the address does not take that method.
That is a 401. A 405 concerns the method and the address, and says nothing about who is calling.
Bad syntax in the body is a 400. A 405 says the method is not supported by the target resource.

choices.label: No route matches the address in the request at all
The address exists but does not accept `POST`
The caller's token is missing or invalid
The body was not valid JSON

questions.prompt: Which of these paths puts a verb in the URL when the method should carry it?
hints: The method already says what to do.
Look for the path that opens with an action.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: /getOrders

questions.onCorrect: A path names a resource, and the method gives the action, so `GET /orders` replaces `/getOrders`.

misconceptions.feedback: /orders names a collection, which is a noun.
/orders/42 names one order, which is a noun.
/orders/42/items names the items of one order, which is a noun.

choices.label: `/orders/42`
`/getOrders`
`/orders`
`/orders/42/items`

questions.prompt: Which JSON value, written as a word, says that a field is present but holds no value?
hints: It is one of three literal words, with true and false.
It is also what a PATCH uses to clear a field.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: null

questions.onCorrect: null marks a field that is present and empty, which differs from a field that is absent and from an empty string.

misconceptions.feedback: JSON has no undefined. A field that is not wanted is simply left out, and a field that is present with no value is written with a different word.
false is a boolean. The word for a missing value is another of the literals.

questions.prompt: An API adds the unit prices `0.10` and `0.20` as JSON numbers and returns `{"total": 0.30000000000000004}`. Which change to the design removes the problem?
hints: The numbers 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be held exactly as binary fractions.
Sums and products of whole numbers are exact.

acceptedIdeas: Hold money as an integer number of cents, so the total is `30`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hold money as an integer number of cents, so the total is `30`

questions.onCorrect: Sums and products of whole numbers are exact, so integer cents cannot drift.

misconceptions.feedback: That hides the symptom, and every client has to repeat the rounding. A sum of whole numbers is exact and needs no repair.
More digits cannot help, because 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form. The extra digits would be just as inexact.
A client that parses the strings into floats gets the same drift. Integer cents are exact for sums and products.

choices.label: Round the total in each client to two decimal places
Hold money as an integer number of cents, so the total is `30`
Send the total with more digits so that it is precise
Send each price as a string such as `"0.10"` and let clients add them

questions.prompt: A response contains `{"id": "7", "qty": "3", "price_cents": 450}`, and the documented type of `qty` is integer. What is wrong?
hints: Compare each value with the type the contract gives it.
A field keeps one type in every response.

acceptedIdeas: `qty` is a string where the contract promises an integer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `qty` is a string where the contract promises an integer

questions.onCorrect: A client is written against the shape of a body, so a field has to keep the type the contract gives it.

misconceptions.feedback: A quoted number is a valid JSON string. The fault is that it is a string where the contract promises an integer.
A JSON parser does not convert types. A client that expects an integer receives a string and may fail or compare it wrongly.
Identifiers are sent as strings so that their form can change later and so that large values survive a double.

choices.label: The body is not valid JSON, because it holds a quoted number
Nothing is wrong, since a JSON parser converts strings to numbers
`qty` is a string where the contract promises an integer
The `id` should be a number, since it is a number in the database

questions.prompt: Which of these is valid JSON?
hints: Look for single quotes, trailing commas and leading zeros.
Only one choice avoids all three.
questions.onCorrect: null is one of JSON's three literal words, so the object parses.

misconceptions.feedback: JSON strings and names need double quotes.
A trailing comma is forbidden in JSON, though JavaScript allows it.
A number may not start with a zero in JSON.

questions.prompt: A client wants an order as JSON. Which request header says which representation it wants?
hints: The client is asking for something in the reply and is not describing a body it sends.
The header lists the media types the client can handle.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Accept

questions.onCorrect: `Accept` lists the representations the client can handle, and `Content-Type` labels the body that is actually sent.

misconceptions.feedback: `Content-Type` describes the body of the message it appears in. The header that asks for a representation in the reply is a different one.

questions.prompt: A parser reads the id `9007199254740993` as a double and returns `9007199254740992`. Why does the value change?
hints: A double has 53 bits for the digits of a number.
Above 2^53 some neighbouring integers have no double of their own.

acceptedIdeas: A double cannot hold every integer above 2^53, so it takes the nearest
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A double cannot hold every integer above 2^53, so it takes the nearest

questions.onCorrect: A double stores integers exactly only up to 2^53, so a larger id is replaced by the nearest value it can hold.

misconceptions.feedback: RFC 8259 sets no such limit. The loss happens when the parser reads the number into a double.
The text on the wire holds the exact digits. The parser changed the value when it converted them to a double.

choices.label: A double cannot hold every integer above 2^53, so it takes the nearest
JSON limits integers to fifteen digits and cuts off the rest
The server sent the digits wrongly, so the parser read what it was given

questions.prompt: The Order schema is an object with properties item (string), qty (integer) and note (string), and required item and qty. Which body is valid?
hints: Both required properties must be present.
Each present property must have its declared type.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: {"item":"pen","qty":3}

questions.onCorrect: The body has both required properties, and each has the declared type. note is optional, so leaving it out is allowed.

misconceptions.feedback: qty is required, and this body does not have it.
qty is present, but "three" is a string, and the schema declares an integer.
item is required, and it is missing. note is optional and does not make up for it.

choices.label: `{"item":"pen","qty":3}`
`{"item":"pen","qty":"three"}`
`{"item":"pen"}`

questions.prompt: Which OpenAPI field gives an operation a unique name that code generators use for a function name?
hints: It sits inside the operation, next to `requestBody` and `responses`.
Its name says what it identifies.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: operationId

questions.onCorrect: `operationId` is unique across the document, so a generator can turn it into a function such as `createOrder`.

misconceptions.feedback: A summary is a short description for people. The field used by code generators as a name is a different one.
The path is the URL, and many operations can share one path under different methods.

questions.prompt: An `Order` schema is the body of a `POST`, the body of a `PUT` and the content of a response. Under which top-level key of the OpenAPI document is it written once, so that each operation refers to it with `$ref`?
hints: The schema is written once and referenced, and is not copied into each operation.
Operations live under `paths`, and the shared parts live under a different key.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: components

questions.onCorrect: A schema written once under `components` means a change to its shape is made in one place and every operation follows it.

misconceptions.feedback: `paths` holds the operations themselves. A schema shared by several operations goes in a separate part of the document that they refer to.

questions.prompt: An OpenAPI description documents only the 201 response of `POST /orders`. What is missing from the contract?
hints: Think about what a client needs to know to write code.
Errors are part of what an operation can return.

acceptedIdeas: The error responses, such as 400, that clients must handle
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The error responses, such as 400, that clients must handle

questions.onCorrect: Error responses are part of the contract, so a client library and its tests can be written for them.

misconceptions.feedback: Errors are part of an API's behaviour, and a client has to handle them.
The request body is declared per operation, and this operation takes one.
A path is always named in the paths section. It is the method that is under it.

choices.label: The request body, which is always optional in OpenAPI
The path, which a client can work out from the method
Nothing, since errors are not part of an API's contract
The error responses, such as 400, that clients must handle

questions.prompt: A collection holds 90 orders and a client asks for 25 at a time. How many pages are there?
hints: Divide the number of orders by the page size.
The division does not come out even.
A partly filled last page still counts as a page.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 90 / 25 = 3.6, which rounds up to 4 pages, the last holding 15.

questions.onCorrect: The page count is the number of items divided by the page size, rounded up, since a partial page is still a page.

misconceptions.feedback: 3 pages of 25 hold only 75 orders. The last 15 need a page of their own.
A page cannot be partly served, so the quotient is rounded up.

questions.prompt: Ids 80 down to 61 are listed newest first. A client asks for `limit=4` and `after=70`. Which ids come back?
hints: `after=70` means: resume after the row with id 70.
The list is newest first, so the next rows have smaller ids.
questions.onCorrect: The page never contains the key itself, only the rows after it.

misconceptions.feedback: The key itself is not part of the page. It names the last row the client already has, and the page starts with the row after it.
Those are the first rows of the list. A request with `after=70` resumes after 70 and does not start again.
The list runs from newest to oldest, so the rows after 70 are the ones with smaller ids.

questions.prompt: Ids 100 down to 91 are listed newest first. A client asks for `limit=3` `after=93`. How many ids are returned?
hints: Find the position of 93 in the list.
Count how many ids come after it.
The page cannot hold more ids than remain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only 92 and 91 come after 93, so 2 are returned.

questions.onCorrect: A keyset page holds up to limit items, and fewer when the list ends first.

misconceptions.feedback: The list ends at 91, so only two ids are left after 93.
There are ids after 93 in the list.

questions.prompt: The server first finds where the key `96` sits in the list. Why does it need that?
hints: The cursor names the last row the client already has.
Ask where the next page has to begin.

acceptedIdeas: The page starts after that key, so the server needs its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The page starts after that key, so the server needs its place

questions.onCorrect: The key marks where the client stopped, so the page begins one place after it.

misconceptions.feedback: The page size is the limit the client sent. The key's place tells the server where to start, and the limit already says how many rows to return.
Authorisation is a separate check. Here the key is only a marker for where to resume.

choices.label: The page starts after that key, so the server needs its place
It needs the key's place to count how many rows the page holds
It must check that the client is allowed to read the row with that key

questions.prompt: A team wants clients to build the cursor themselves, for example `cursor=id:70`, so that they can jump to any position. Why do APIs keep the cursor opaque instead?
hints: Think about what a client that builds its own cursors comes to depend on.
The lesson says a server may add a sort key, a filter or a signature to the cursor later.

acceptedIdeas: The server can add a sort key or a signature without breaking clients
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The server can add a sort key or a signature without breaking clients

questions.onCorrect: A client that only hands the cursor back leaves the server free to change what it holds.

misconceptions.feedback: The client does send it back to get the next page. Opaque means the client does not look inside it.
Speed is not the reason. A client that builds cursors depends on their contents, and then the server can no longer change them.

choices.label: The server can add a sort key or a signature without breaking clients
The client never sends the cursor back to the server, so its form does not matter
A cursor that the client builds is slower for the database to use

questions.prompt: A client reads a newest-first list in pages of 10 with `offset`, and fetches page 1 and then page 2. For each change made between the two requests, what does the client see?
hints: Ask whether the change happens before page 2 begins or after it.
A row added in front pushes later rows along, and a row removed in front pulls them back.

items.label: A new row is added at the top of the list
items.explanation: Every row moves one place down, so the last row of page 1 is the first row of page 2.

items.label: Three new rows are added at the top of the list
items.explanation: Three rows shift down, so page 2 starts with three rows from page 1.

items.label: A row on page 1 is deleted
items.explanation: The first row of page 2 moves up into page 1's range, and the client never sees it.

items.label: A row on page 3 is deleted
items.explanation: It lies after page 2, so nothing in front of the offset moves.

items.label: A new row is added at the very end of the list
items.explanation: Nothing in front of page 2 moves.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rows added at the top are repeated on page 2, a row deleted from page 1 makes the client skip one, and changes after page 2 do no harm.

questions.onCorrect: Offset paging counts from the start, so any change in front of the page shifts what the offset points at.

questions.prompt: Which way of paging survives rows being inserted at the front of the list between requests?
hints: Which method marks a row and not a count?
A key stays attached to its row.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keyset paging with a cursor

questions.onCorrect: A key names a row, so rows inserted in front do not move it, whereas an offset counts from the start.

misconceptions.feedback: A larger limit only changes the page size. An offset still counts from the start.
Requesting twice does not remove the shift that an insertion causes.
Page 1 never reaches the later rows.

choices.label: Keyset paging with a cursor
Asking for page 1 repeatedly
Offset paging, but requested twice
Offset paging with a larger limit

questions.prompt: A client sends `POST /charges` for 25 with `Idempotency-Key: 7f3a`, and the connection drops before the response arrives. It retries with the same key. What should the server do with the second request?
hints: The key names one logical operation, not one attempt.
The server stored the result under the key the first time it acted.

acceptedIdeas: Return the stored response of the first, without charging again
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Return the stored response of the first, without charging again

questions.onCorrect: Retries become harmless, which is what lets a client send them freely after a timeout.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fault the key exists to prevent. The server has seen this key and must not act twice.
A retry with the same key and the same body is expected. The server answers it with the stored result, so the client learns how the first request ended.
The client sent the key so that its retry would be recognised. A new key would be a new operation, and so a second charge.

choices.label: Charge again, since the server treats every `POST` as a new request
Return the stored response of the first, without charging again
Reject it with a `400`, since the key has been used before
Wait for the client to send a new key and act on that instead

questions.prompt: A client sends a charge and the request times out. It sends the same charge again, and then a second, different charge. Which keys should the three requests carry?
hints: A key names one logical operation, and every retry of that operation repeats it.
Ask what the server would do with a retry that arrived under a new key.

acceptedIdeas: The first two share one key, and the third has its own
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first two share one key, and the third has its own

questions.onCorrect: A key names one operation, so every retry of it carries the same key and a different operation gets a new one.

misconceptions.feedback: The second charge is a different operation. Under the same key the server would see a different body, or treat the new charge as a repeat and never carry it out.
A retry with a new key looks like a new operation, so the server would charge a second time.
The client generates the key before it sends anything, because a lost reply cannot carry a key back.

choices.label: All three share one key, so the server does the work once
The first two share one key, and the third has its own
Each has its own key, so that no two are ever confused
The server chooses the keys and returns one in each reply

questions.prompt: The key `k1` arrives a second time. What does the server do with it?
hints: The server stored a result under `k1` after the first request.
Ask what a client that retried needs to learn.

acceptedIdeas: It returns the stored response and charges nothing more
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It returns the stored response and charges nothing more

questions.onCorrect: The second `k1` is recognised as a retry, so the server returns what it stored and does not charge again.

misconceptions.feedback: The server stored a result under `k1` the first time, so the second arrival is recognised as a repeat.
A repeat with the same key and the same body is a retry, and it gets the stored response. A rejection is for the same key with a different body.

choices.label: It returns the stored response and charges nothing more
It charges 40 again, since the request is a new one
It rejects the request with `409`, since the key is already in use

questions.prompt: The server receives (p, 25), (q, 5), (p, 25), (r, 10) in order, and charges only the first sight of a key. How much is charged in total?
hints: p is seen first, and its repeat is ignored.
q and r are new keys.
Add 25, 5 and 10.
questions.onCorrect: Each key is charged once, however often it arrives.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the repeat of p as well. A repeat of a key is ignored.
The request for r is charged too.

questions.prompt: Which member of a problem-details body holds a stable, machine-readable identifier of the kind of error?
hints: It is usually a URI.
The client's code branches on it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: type

questions.onCorrect: type stays the same for every occurrence of one kind of error, so a client can react without parsing any text.

misconceptions.feedback: The title is a short name for a person to read. The member that code can rely on is another one.
The detail describes this particular case, and its wording may change. Code should not rely on it.

questions.prompt: Two requests with the same `Idempotency-Key` reach the server at the same moment, before either has finished. The server checks whether it has seen the key, then charges, then stores the key. What can go wrong?
hints: Ask what the second request sees at the moment it checks.
Two steps with a gap between them can be interleaved with another request.

acceptedIdeas: Both checks find no key, so both requests charge
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both checks find no key, so both requests charge

questions.onCorrect: The check and the store have to be one atomic step, for instance a unique constraint on the key, so that only one request can claim it.

misconceptions.feedback: The network does not know about keys. Only the server's own check can recognise a repeat.
A database runs statements in order only if the code asks it to. A check followed by a separate store leaves a gap in which both requests pass the check.
The harm is the second charge made in the gap before the key is stored, whatever happens to the key afterwards.

choices.label: Both checks find no key, so both requests charge
The second request is rejected by the network as a duplicate
Nothing, because the database runs the two requests one after the other
The key is stored twice, which does no harm

questions.prompt: Which media type does RFC 9457 give for a problem-details body?
hints: It is a media type, so it has a type and a subtype.
It names the problem format and JSON.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: application/problem+json

questions.onCorrect: The media type lets a client recognise the body as a problem-details object before it reads any member.

misconceptions.feedback: A plain JSON type would not tell a client that the body is a problem description. RFC 9457 defines a more specific type.

questions.prompt: A server receives `POST /charges` with a key it has not seen. In what order does it handle the request?
hints: The server can only act on a key after it has checked it.
Ask what a retry would find if the response were sent before it was stored.

items: It looks the key up and finds nothing stored
It carries out the charge
It stores the response under the key
It sends the response to the client

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The server finds no stored result, carries out the charge, stores the response under the key, and only then sends it.

questions.onCorrect: The result is stored before it is sent, so a retry after a lost response finds it.

questions.prompt: Which change is non-breaking for existing clients?
hints: Ask whether an old client could still do everything it did before.
Three of the four take something away or demand something new.

acceptedIdeas: Adding an optional field to a response
