questions.prompt: Why does the operation list a 400 response as well as a 201?
hints: Ask what a client written from this document would do when a request has an invalid body.
A document that lists only the success response leaves the client to guess about the rest.

acceptedIdeas: A client must handle failures as well as success, so the contract lists both
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A client must handle failures as well as success, so the contract lists both

questions.onCorrect: The operation documents 201 and 400, so a client can handle both without reading the server's code.

choices.label: A client must handle failures as well as success, so the contract lists both
A 400 response is required whenever an operation has a request body
A 201 response cannot be documented without some second response listed beside it

misconceptions.feedback: OpenAPI does not demand any particular error response. Listing it is a choice that comes from what clients need.
Each response is documented on its own. A 201 can stand alone as the description of success.

questions.prompt: The `Order` schema requires `item` (a string) and `qty` (an integer). How many errors does a validator report for the body `{"item":5,"qty":2.5}`?
hints: Check each required property for presence first.
Then check the type of each value against the schema.
2.5 is a number, but it is not a whole number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both required properties are present. item is the number 5, where a string is declared, and qty is 2.5, which is not an integer: 2 errors.

questions.onCorrect: Each present property is checked against its declared type, and both values fail, so the validator reports two errors.

misconceptions.feedback: Both properties are present, but presence is not the only check. Look at the type of each value.
Check both values against their declared types, and not only one of them.

questions.prompt: A list of products is sorted by price, cheapest first, and several products cost 4.99. The last product a client saw costs 4.99 and has id 12. What should the cursor hold so that the next page starts in exactly the right place?
hints: The cursor has to name one exact place in the sorted order.
Ask what two products with the same price have that tells them apart.

acceptedIdeas: The price and the id of the last product
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The price and the id of the last product

questions.onCorrect: The price gives the place in the order, and the unique id settles the products that tie on it, so the pair names one exact row.

choices.label: The price, 4.99, as the last product had it
The id, 12, of the last product seen
The price and the id of the last product

misconceptions.feedback: Several products share the price 4.99, so the price alone does not name one place in the order, and rows can be skipped or repeated.
The list is sorted by price and not by id, so the id alone does not say where in the order the last product sits.

questions.prompt: A handler is writing the error body for a failed charge. Which member should it not send to the caller?
hints: Think about what would help an attacker.
Which of these shows how the server works inside?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `"detail": "charges.py line 88: SELECT * FROM cards"`

questions.onCorrect: A file name, a line number and a SQL statement show how the server is built, so they belong in its own logs and not in a response.

choices.label: `"title": "The card was declined"`
`"detail": "charges.py line 88: SELECT * FROM cards"`
`"detail": "The expiry date is in the past."`
`"type": "https://api.shop.example/problems/card-declined"`

misconceptions.feedback: A short title is for a person to read. This one describes the problem and shows nothing about the server.
A detail may say what the client can fix. An expired date is exactly that, and it shows nothing about the server.
A type is a stable name for the kind of error. It is an identifier and not a view into the server.

questions.prompt: Why does the response keep `qty` while `quantity` is added?
hints: Ask who still reads the old name during the migration.
Ask what would happen to those readers if the old field vanished on day one.

acceptedIdeas: Old clients still read `qty` and would fail if it vanished
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Old clients still read `qty` and would fail if it vanished

questions.onCorrect: Serving both lets old clients keep reading `qty` while new clients move to `quantity`.

choices.label: Old clients still read `qty` and would fail if it vanished
New clients need both fields to work out the quantity correctly
A response must keep every field name it has ever used, for ever

misconceptions.feedback: New clients read `quantity` and ignore `qty`. They do not need the old name.
A field can be removed once no client reads it. Nothing requires old names to stay for ever.

questions.prompt: The handler has loaded invoice 18 for caller 9. What must it compare with the caller's id before it returns the invoice?
hints: The handler already has the caller's id from the token. It needs something from the invoice to compare it with.
The check asks whether the caller is the person who owns this invoice.

acceptedIdeas: The id of the user who owns the invoice
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The id of the user who owns the invoice

questions.onCorrect: The handler loads the object and compares its owner with the authenticated caller.

choices.label: The id of the invoice, 18
The caller's own id from the token, which is 9
The id of the user who owns the invoice

misconceptions.feedback: That is the invoice's own id. It names the invoice and says nothing about who may have it.
Comparing the caller with their own id would always match, and it would prove nothing.

questions.prompt: `DELETE /documents/{id}` deletes a document whenever the caller is logged in. Which fix addresses the flaw?
hints: The flaw is that any logged-in caller can delete any document.
Which change refuses a caller who does not own it?

acceptedIdeas: Check that the caller owns the document
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Check that the caller owns the document

questions.onCorrect: The server has to compare the owner of the object with the caller on every request.

choices.label: Use longer, random document ids
Check that the caller owns the document
Hide the delete button in the page for other users
Require HTTPS on every request

misconceptions.feedback: Longer ids make guessing harder, but a caller who learns an id can still use it.
A hidden button does not stop a request. The server enforces the rule, and the page does not.
HTTPS protects the data in transit. It does not decide whose document it is.

questions.prompt: A handler runs `SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?` and sends the value `'; DROP TABLE users; --` separately as a parameter. What does the database do with that value?
hints: Ask whether the database ever reads the value as part of the query.
The value is sent separately from the query text.

acceptedIdeas: It compares the value as an ordinary name, so no row matches
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It compares the value as an ordinary name, so no row matches

questions.onCorrect: The value is compared as an ordinary string, so the query looks for a user with exactly that name, and none exists.

choices.label: It runs the `DROP TABLE` statement before the comparison
It rejects the query as malformed because of the semicolon in it
It compares the value as an ordinary name, so no row matches

misconceptions.feedback: That happens when the value is joined into the query text. A parameter is sent separately, so the database never treats any part of it as query syntax.
The semicolon is only a character in the value. The database does not parse the value as part of the query, so nothing about it is malformed.

questions.prompt: A client retries six times. The first wait is 300 ms, and each wait doubles the one before it, but no wait is longer than 4000 ms. What is the total waiting time in milliseconds?
hints: Write out the waits one by one, doubling each time.
A wait that would pass 4000 is held at 4000.
Add the six waits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The waits are 300, 600, 1200, 2400, 4000 and 4000 ms, because doubling would give 4800 and 9600 for the last two and the cap holds each at 4000. They add up to 12500 ms.

questions.onCorrect: The cap limits the fifth and sixth waits to 4000 ms, so the total is smaller than with doubling alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 4800 and 9600 for the last two waits. The cap holds each at 4000.
That is the total of the first five waits. The sixth adds another 4000.
That adds only the four waits that stay below the cap. There are two more.

questions.prompt: The worker writes a log line for each event: `email sent order=20`, `email sent order=21`, `skip repeat order=20` and `ignore created order=22`. What does the last event, `(22, paid)`, add to the log?
hints: The worker emails an order the first time it sees a paid event for it.
The earlier event for order 22 was a created event, which sends nothing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `email sent order=22`

questions.onCorrect: Order 22's paid event is the first one for that order, so the worker sends the email.

misconceptions.feedback: Order 22 has not been emailed yet. Its earlier event was a created event, which sends nothing and records nothing.
That line was written for the earlier event. This one is a paid event, which sends the email.
A created event does not count as having emailed the order. The first paid event for order 22 is its first chance to send.

choices.label: `skip repeat order=22`
`ignore created order=22`
Nothing, because order 22 was seen in the previous event
`email sent order=22`

questions.prompt: The service is running, but its database is down for two minutes. Restarting the service would not help, and it should not receive traffic until the database is back. Which check should report the failure?
hints: One check decides whether the process is restarted, and the other decides whether it is sent traffic.
A process can be running and still unable to do its work.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The readiness check

questions.onCorrect: A readiness check also confirms what the service depends on, so it fails while the database is down and the service stays out of rotation without being restarted.

choices.label: The health check alone
Both checks together
The readiness check

misconceptions.feedback: A health check says the process is up, and the process is up. Failing it would make the platform restart a service that a restart cannot fix.
A failing health check would trigger a restart that does not help here, so only one of the two checks should fail.

flashcards.front: Which request header names the server being asked, such as `shop.example`?
flashcards.back: Host, because one machine can serve many sites and the request line holds only the path.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Host

flashcards.front: How many bytes does the single letter é take in UTF-8?
flashcards.back: Two bytes, because it lies outside the ASCII range.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two bytes, because it lies outside the ASCII range.

flashcards.front: Why does the server never see the part of an address after the #?
flashcards.back: The fragment is used by the browser to scroll to a place in the page, so it is not put in the request.

flashcards.front: Which method replaces the resource at a known address with the body sent?
flashcards.back: PUT, which states the end value, so repeating it changes nothing further.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: PUT

flashcards.front: What word describes a method whose repeated requests leave the server in the same state as one request?
flashcards.back: Idempotent. GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, and POST is not.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: idempotent

flashcards.front: Why can a client not tell a lost request from a lost response?
flashcards.back: In both cases it receives nothing, so it cannot know whether the server acted, which is why only safe or idempotent requests may be repeated automatically.

flashcards.front: Which status code means created, and goes with a Location header?
flashcards.back: 201 Created.

flashcards.front: Which status code means the caller has not been identified (missing or invalid credentials)?
flashcards.back: 401, which is about authentication despite the word Unauthorized in its name.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 401, which is about authentication despite the word Unauthorized in its name.

flashcards.front: Why should an API not answer every request with 200?
flashcards.back: Clients, caches, monitoring and retry logic read the status code before the body, so a 200 on an error tells them everything succeeded.

flashcards.front: Which request header does a cache send to check a stale copy against the ETag it stored?
flashcards.back: If-None-Match, which asks the origin to send the body only if the version is no longer the stored one.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: If-None-Match

flashcards.front: Which status code lets a cache reuse its copy, with no body sent?
flashcards.back: 304 Not Modified.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between no-cache and no-store?
flashcards.back: no-cache lets a cache keep a copy but requires revalidation before reuse, whereas no-store forbids keeping the response at all.

flashcards.front: Which part of a URL narrows or shapes the result, such as `?status=open`?
flashcards.back: The query, which is sent in the request line after the path.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: query

flashcards.front: Name the method that adds a new item to a collection such as /orders.
flashcards.back: POST, since the server picks the new item's address.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: POST

flashcards.front: Why is `POST /orders/42/cancellation` a better design than `GET /orders/42/cancel`?
flashcards.back: A GET is meant to be safe and software sends it freely, so a GET that cancels an order could be triggered by a crawler or a prefetch.

flashcards.front: Name the JSON literal that marks a field as present but empty.
flashcards.back: null.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: null

flashcards.front: A price of 12.50 is held as integer cents. How many cents is it?
Why should an id that may exceed 2^53 be sent as a string?
flashcards.back: A parser that reads JSON numbers as doubles cannot hold integers above 2^53 exactly, so the id could silently change.

flashcards.front: Which OpenAPI field names an operation for code generators?
flashcards.back: `operationId`.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: operationId

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a required property and a nullable one?
flashcards.back: Required means the property must be present in the body, while nullable means its value may be null, and the two are stated separately.

flashcards.front: Why is a drifting description a defect?
flashcards.back: Tools generate clients, mocks and tests from it, so a description that disagrees with the server breaks the code built on it.

flashcards.front: What do you call the opaque token that tells a server where to resume a list?
flashcards.back: A cursor, which the client hands back unchanged.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: cursor

flashcards.front: Which paging scheme resumes after the last key the client saw, and survives rows added at the front?
flashcards.back: Keyset paging, which an API usually hides inside a cursor.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: keyset

flashcards.front: Why does offset paging repeat rows when new rows are added at the front?
flashcards.back: The offset counts from the start of the list, so each new row pushes the later rows along by one place and the second page begins on rows already seen.

flashcards.front: Which header carries the client's unique key for making a POST safe to retry?
flashcards.back: Idempotency-Key, which the server stores with the response so that a repeat returns the stored result.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Idempotency-Key

flashcards.front: Which media type does RFC 9457 give for an error body?
flashcards.back: application/problem+json.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: application/problem+json

flashcards.front: What happens when a request arrives with a key the server has seen but a different body?
flashcards.back: The client has made a mistake, because one key must always mean one request, so the server rejects it with an error such as 422 or 409.

flashcards.front: Why is adding an optional response field not a breaking change?
flashcards.back: A client written against the old contract reads the fields it knows and ignores any it does not, so a new field leaves it working.

flashcards.front: A response drops the field `qty` and adds `quantity`. Is that a breaking change, and how is it made safely?
flashcards.back: Yes, because clients that read `qty` fail. Serve both fields, announce a Sunset date for `qty`, and remove it when nobody reads it.

flashcards.front: Name the response header that gives the date after which something is removed.
flashcards.back: Sunset, which lets clients plan their move before the date.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sunset

flashcards.front: Which status code reports missing or invalid credentials?
flashcards.back: 401, which is about authentication despite its name.

flashcards.front: What does a random salt stop in a table of password hashes?
flashcards.back: Two users with the same password having the same hash, and one precomputed table cracking every row.

flashcards.front: Why is a signed token's payload not secret?
flashcards.back: The signature only proves the payload has not been changed. Base64 is an encoding, so anyone holding the token can read the payload.

flashcards.front: What is it called when a request for a specific object is not checked against who owns it?
flashcards.back: Broken object level authorisation, the first item in the OWASP API Security Top 10 of 2023.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: broken object level authorisation

flashcards.front: What fix keeps input as data and out of a database query's structure?
flashcards.back: A parameterised query, which sends the value separately from the query text.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: parameterised query

flashcards.front: Why is hiding a button not authorisation?
flashcards.back: A client can send any request it likes, so the server has to enforce every rule itself.

flashcards.front: Which status code does a server send when a client is over its rate limit?
flashcards.back: 429 Too Many Requests, which may carry a Retry-After header.

flashcards.front: Delays start at 100 ms and double. What is the fourth delay in milliseconds?
What does a token bucket allow that a fixed count per second does not?
flashcards.back: A burst up to the capacity, because unused tokens accumulate, together with a steady rate over time set by the refill.

flashcards.front: Which layer of a service applies business rules and opens the transaction?
flashcards.back: The service layer, which keeps both free of HTTP and of SQL.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: service

flashcards.front: What delivery guarantee does a retrying queue give?
flashcards.back: At-least-once, so a consumer may see a message twice.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: at-least-once

flashcards.front: Why should a consumer keep the ids of messages it has handled?
flashcards.back: The queue may deliver a message more than once, and the ids let the consumer skip repeats so that the effect happens once.
